opus-5.5.text:
I think in the long run, yes, they should converge, though maybe not in the way people usually imagine.

If you look at it from first principles, what all three are trying to do is the same thing: build a system that can perceive the world, understand it, reason about it, and then act in it. Multimodal models are mostly focused on the perceive-and-understand part, and recently on reasoning. Autonomous driving is a very specific, very constrained form of acting in the world. Robotics is the more general form of acting. So conceptually they're different slices of the same problem.

But right now they're on quite different technical paths, and I think that's for practical reasons, not fundamental ones. Autonomous driving has a huge amount of data, a well-defined action space, and strong commercial pressure, so it's developed its own end-to-end stack that's very optimized for that one task. Robotics has the opposite problem: the action space is enormous and the data is very scarce, so people borrow heavily from vision-language models to get some common sense for free. And multimodal models have the internet's data but almost no grounding in physical consequences.

What I expect is that the core, which is essentially a model that understands the world and can reason over long horizons, will become shared. Something like a foundation model that has learned both from internet-scale multimodal data and from interaction data. Then on top of it you have different "bodies": a car is one kind of body, a humanoid or a robot arm is another, and a chatbot is, in a sense, a body whose only action is producing text. The embodiment-specific parts, like control, low-level policies, and safety constraints, will probably stay specialized for a long time.

There's one more thing I'd say. I don't think pure multimodal understanding alone gets you to AGI. A model that has only watched and read the world is missing something that comes from acting and seeing the consequences, which is how you learn causality and not just correlation. So in a way, driving and robotics aren't just applications of AGI; they may be part of how we get there, because they provide the feedback loop that static data can't. The convergence goes both ways: the general model makes robots smarter, and the robots' experience makes the general model more grounded.

So my answer is: the same brain, many bodies. But we're still fairly early, and the timeline for robotics in particular is probably longer than the current excitement suggests.

r001.rationale: The response says autonomous driving has a well-defined action space while robotics has an enormous one, but does not clearly attribute autonomous driving’s earlier development to that constraint.

r002.rationale: It predicts convergence around a shared model, but does not clearly predict that fully end-to-end systems incorporating visual or multimodal reasoning will converge on AGI.

r003.rationale: It describes current differences as practical rather than fundamental and links robotics’ challenges to its enormous action space and scarce data, implying current limitations rather than an inherent endpoint.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they will converge, but not in the way people usually imagine, where you take a big language model, bolt on a camera, and call it a day. My view is that the convergence happens at the level of the learning paradigm, not the architecture or the product.

Let me explain what I mean. If you look at how language models got to where they are, the key was a combination of massive scale, a very simple objective, and a data source that happened to be enormous and already compressed by humans. Text is special in that sense: it is the output of human thinking, so you get a lot of reasoning for free. Vision, driving, and robotics do not have that luxury. The raw signal is far noisier, the useful information per byte is much lower, and the hardest part, which is the decision-making loop, is not written down anywhere. Nobody has produced trillions of tokens describing exactly what torque to apply to a joint.

So in the short term, these three fields look very different. Multimodal models today are mostly perception plus language. Autonomous driving is a closed-world problem with a strong engineering flavor, where the long tail dominates and reliability matters more than generality. Robotics is the most open and the most data-starved. If you only look at the current systems, you would say they are three separate disciplines.

But if you ask what AGI actually requires, I think the answer is a system that can perceive, act, get feedback from the world, and improve from that feedback without a human writing down the lesson. That is fundamentally a reinforcement-learning-style loop, or at least a world-model-style loop, rather than pure imitation. And once you frame it that way, driving and robotics are not side problems. They are the places where the environment pushes back and tells you when you are wrong. Language models are, in a sense, missing that. They learned from a frozen snapshot of human output and only recently started getting real feedback through RL on verifiable tasks.

So my prediction is this. The form of AGI will not be "a language model that also sees." It will be a general learner whose core is about building internal models of the world and using them to act, and language will be one of its interfaces rather than its foundation. Multimodal models are approaching that from the top down, starting with abstraction and trying to ground it. Driving and robotics are approaching it from the bottom up, starting with grounding and trying to generalize. I believe they meet in the middle, and when they meet, the distinctions we draw today will look a bit like how we once separated computer vision into detection, segmentation, and tracking as if they were different sciences.

One caveat I would add: convergence in paradigm does not mean one model will run everything. A car has latency constraints and safety requirements that a chatbot does not. There will be specialization at deployment time. But the way these systems are trained, the way they represent the world, and the way they improve, I think those will become the same story. And honestly, the part I find most interesting is that the embodied problems might end up teaching the language side more than the other way around, because they force you to confront what it means to actually understand something rather than describe it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts autonomous driving as a closed-world problem with robotics as open and data-starved, but does not say driving will develop earlier or attribute that timing to its more constrained control problem.

r002.rationale: The response predicts convergence in the learning paradigm while explicitly distinguishing that from convergence in architecture or product. It does not predict that fully end-to-end visual or multimodal systems will converge on the same form as AGI.

r003.rationale: The response describes robotics as open and data-starved, but does not discuss current robots’ narrow specialization or say that it results from technological limitations rather than an inherent endpoint.

astra-6.text:
I think they’ll converge in some respects, but I wouldn’t assume they’ll end up in exactly the same form. Multimodal models, autonomous driving, and robotics share a basic challenge: understanding an environment and figuring out how to respond. A more general intelligence could provide a common foundation for all three.

But the demands are different. A model having a conversation can make a mistake and be corrected. A car or a robot has to act in the physical world, where timing matters and mistakes can have immediate consequences. So even if they share a core model, they may still need very different ways of controlling actions and ensuring reliability.

The question, to me, is whether the underlying capabilities transfer. Can something learned through language or video help a robot handle an unfamiliar situation? Can experience acting in the world improve the model’s understanding? If those connections become strong enough, that would be a meaningful kind of convergence. It doesn’t necessarily mean everything becomes one identical system.

r001.rationale: It says cars and robots face different physical-world demands, but does not attribute autonomous driving developing earlier than general-purpose robotics to a more constrained control problem.

r002.rationale: It allows for a shared foundation, but says convergence need not mean one identical system and does not predict that end-to-end visual or multimodal systems will converge on AGI’s form.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss current robots’ specialization or explain it as a result of technological limitations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they may converge at the level of underlying capabilities, but not necessarily into the same form. Multimodal models learn relationships across language, images, and sound. Autonomous-driving systems and robots also have to act: they must make decisions, deal with uncertainty, and learn from what happens in the physical world.

There is a lot of overlap. All of them need to understand their environment, predict what might happen, and generalize to unfamiliar situations. But shared capabilities don’t mean identical systems. Driving has very specific constraints, while a general-purpose robot faces a much broader range of tasks.

So I would distinguish a common foundation from a common final product. We may develop increasingly general models that support all these applications, while the systems built around them remain quite different. Whether that foundation becomes AGI depends on whether it can reliably transfer what it learns across tasks—not simply whether it can process more kinds of input.

r001.rationale: The response says driving has specific constraints and robotics covers broader tasks, but it does not claim that constrained control lets autonomous driving develop earlier than general-purpose robotics.

r002.rationale: It allows convergence in underlying capabilities while explicitly saying systems may not take the same form; it does not predict that fully end-to-end visual or multimodal systems will converge on AGI’s form.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe current robots as narrowly specialized or attribute that specialization to technological limitations.
